frames: {b} brings {a} before the elders: in a quarrel at {place}, {a} {@injury}. {@demand}.

options.text: struck {b} with a rock. {b} did not die but lay bedridden for six weeks before walking with a staff
struck {b} with a rock and destroyed one of {b:his} eyes for good
options.ev: permanent loss of an eye confirmed

options.text: struck {b} in the face with a rock and knocked out {b:his} front tooth
options.ev: permanent loss of a tooth confirmed

options.text: {b} demands that {a}'s own leg be broken in literal retaliation
{b}'s family demands that {a} suffer exactly the same injury

hint: Compare what the injured man has lost: only time and health, or something that will never come back.

time.label: Compensate Lost Time & Full Medical Care
time.summary: Order {a} to pay {b}'s lost wages and healing costs until fully recovered.

damages.label: Assess Proportional Damages for the Loss
damages.summary: Order {a} to pay damages equal to the permanent harm, plus all healing costs.

literal.label: Inflict the Identical Injury on {a}
literal.summary: Enforce literal bodily retaliation by maiming {a} in exactly the way {b} was hurt.

stripes.label: Flog {a} Without Payment
stripes.summary: Administer 39 stripes to {a} in public and dismiss the financial claim entirely.

dismiss.label: Dismiss Both Claims
dismiss.summary: Rule that mutual quarrelling voids any right to recovery for either man.

rules.rationale: When the victim recovers, Exodus 21:18–19 requires the assailant to pay for the lost time and complete healing. Lex talionis is a principle of proportional damages, not literal mutilation.

blessing.title: Vengeance Capped
blessing.effect: Quarrels end with repayment instead of a cycle of maiming.

rules.rationale: For a permanent injury, 'eye for eye, tooth for tooth' (Exod 21:24; Lev 24:19–20; Deut 19:21) sets a measure: the court assesses damages equal to the harm, no more and no less, in addition to healing costs.

blessing.title: Proportion Preserved
blessing.effect: The penalty matches the harm; no one is mutilated and no one is under-compensated.

titles: The Master Who Struck His Servant
frames: At {town}, a bondservant's household brings a complaint: {@outcome}. {m} argues that a master may do as he pleases with his own household.
{s}'s kin bring {m} before the elders. {@outcome}. {m} claims that no penalty applies to a master.

options.text: in a rage {m} struck {s}, {m:his} bondservant, across the face and destroyed one eye
{m} knocked out one of {s}'s teeth in a fit of temper
{m} beat {s}, {m:his} bondservant, with a rod and {s} died under {m:his} hand
{m} beat {s}, {m:his} bondservant, with a rod; {s} lingered a day or two and then died
options.ev: servant survived a day or two
options.w: Servant Survived a Day or Two

hint: The Torah protects bondservants, but the remedy differs for lasting injury, immediate death, and later death.

free.label: Set the Servant Free for the Injury

avenge.label: Avenge the Servant's Death
avenge.summary: Hold {m} answerable for the killing as for any homicide.

later.label: No Vengeance: the Master Bears the Loss
later.summary: Decline to avenge, since the servant survived a day or two and the loss is {m}'s own.

literal.label: Gouge Out the Master's Eye
literal.summary: Apply literal Lex Talionis and keep the servant bound.

dismiss.label: Dismiss: a Master Is Immune
dismiss.summary: Rule that a master answers for nothing unless the servant dies on the spot.

fine.label: Fine the Master 15 Shekels
fine.summary: Leave the servant in bondage and fine the master.

rules.rationale: In stark contrast to the Code of Hammurabi, which treated servants as chattel, Exodus 21:26–27 gives immediate, unconditional freedom to a servant whose eye or even a single tooth is destroyed by his master.

blessing.title: A Servant's Dignity Upheld
blessing.effect: Masters learn that a servant's body is not their property to destroy.

rules.rationale: If a servant dies under the master's hand, the master is to be avenged upon (Exod 21:20); the killing is not treated as a mere loss of property.

blessing.title: No One Above the Law
blessing.effect: Even a master's authority cannot excuse a killing.

rules.rationale: If the servant survives a day or two, the text declines vengeance because the servant is the master's own property and loss (Exod 21:21). It distinguishes this from death on the spot.

blessing.title: The Text Applied as Written
blessing.effect: The court holds to the text's careful distinction.

titles: The Brawl by the Spice Stalls
frames: At {town}, {a} and {b} brawled near the spice stalls and knocked down {h}'s pregnant wife {w}, causing a premature birth. {@outcome}. {h} demands harsh justice.
{h} brings {a} and {b} before the elders. In their brawl, {h}'s pregnant wife {w} was knocked down and gave birth early. {@outcome}. {h} demands harsh justice.

options.text: Midwives confirm that neither mother nor child suffered lasting injury or death
Midwives report that {w} lost the sight of one eye in the fall
Midwives report that {w} died of her injuries

hint: The remedy depends entirely on the outcome for the mother and child.

fine.label: Court-Approved Monetary Fine
fine.summary: Require the fighters to pay the fine {h} requests, as moderated by the judges.

talion.label: Apply Lex Talionis Matching the Harm
talion.summary: Assess the penalty the harm requires: life for life, eye for eye, no more.

execute.label: Execute Both Brawlers ('Life for Life')
execute.summary: Impose capital punishment automatically, whatever the medical outcome.

exile.label: Exile Both Fighters to a City of Refuge
exile.summary: Treat the scuffle as manslaughter and send both men to a refuge city.

acquit.label: Acquit Completely
acquit.summary: Dismiss the case against both men with no penalty at all.

rules.rationale: Exodus 21:22 prescribes a fine proposed by the husband and moderated by the judges when the premature birth causes no further harm; 'life for life, eye for eye' (vv. 23–25) applies only when serious injury or death follows.

blessing.title: Penalty Fits the Harm
blessing.effect: The fighters pay, the family is satisfied, and no one is maimed over a scuffle.

rules.rationale: When serious injury or death follows, Exodus 21:23–25 applies the full scale: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, with the judges ensuring the penalty matches the harm exactly.

blessing.title: Measure for Measure
blessing.effect: The harm is answered in proportion, neither more nor less.

frames: At {town}, {b} accuses {a} of killing {b}'s {@animal}: {a} {@deed}. {b} demands {a}'s life in return.
{b} brings {a} before the elders. {a} {@deed}, and {b}'s {@animal} is dead. {b} demands blood for blood.
witness: Two Witnesses to the Killing of the Animal

options.text: struck it down in a rage
drove it over the edge of a ravine in a fit of temper

hint: Read 'life for life' in the Torah's own words when the victim is an animal.

replace.label: Replace the Animal, Life for Life
replace.summary: Order {a} to give {b} a living animal of equal worth in its place.

execute.label: Execute {a} for the Beast's Life
execute.summary: Take a human life for the animal's life, applying blood-for-blood to a beast.

dismiss.label: Dismiss: Beasts Are Mere Property
dismiss.summary: Rule that no remedy lies for the death of a beast, since animals have no standing at law.

stripes.label: Flog {a} and Order No Payment
stripes.summary: Give {a} stripes for his temper and award {b} nothing for the loss of the animal.

double.label: Order Double Restitution
double.summary: Require {a} to pay {b} twice the animal's value as a penalty for the killing.

rules.rationale: 'Whoever takes an animal's life shall make it good, life for life' (Lev 24:18, 21): he replaces the animal with one of equal worth. Lex talionis for an animal means exact replacement, not the offender's death.

blessing.title: Fair Replacement
blessing.effect: The owner is made whole and the quarrel ends without bloodshed.
